slides: I want to use the last question to show you three objects that show up on the exam every now and then. If you know them by heart, you save precious time.

slides.say: The first one is square, circle, square. A square, a circle inside it, and a square inside the circle. It's exactly the case we just solved.
We saw that the big square is made of eight identical triangles, and the small square of four. So the outer square's area is always twice the inner square's area.
at: the outer square's area is always twice

slides: A question like the last one comes near the end of the section, and it has appeared a few times. If you know this, you mark the answer at once.

slides.say: It's also worth knowing the sides. With a radius of one, the outer side is two, and the inner side is root two. Two is root two times root two, so the outer side is root two times the inner side.
at: the outer side is root two times

slides.say: The second one is circle, square, circle. A circle, a square inside it, and a circle inside the square. It's almost the same case.
Why? Say the small radius is one. The small circle touches the square's sides, so the square's side is a diameter, two.
at: Say the small radius is one

slides.say: The square's diagonal makes a silver triangle with two sides, and in a silver triangle the hypotenuse is the leg times root two. So the diagonal is two root two. And that diagonal is a diameter of the big circle, so the big radius is half of it, root two.
at: so the big radius is half

slides.say: So the outer radius is root two times the inner radius. Now the areas. The small circle is pi times one squared, pi. The big circle is pi times root two, squared, which is two pi.
So again, the outer circle's area is exactly twice the inner circle's area.
The third and last one is triangle, circle, triangle. But only with equilateral triangles.
Here it's different. The outer triangle isn't twice the inner one, it's four times as big. And the outer side is twice the inner side.

Why? The circle touches each side of the big triangle right in its middle, because the equilateral triangle is symmetric. Turn the small triangle upside down, like here. Turning it doesn't change its size. Now its corners touch those middles.
So the big triangle is cut into four equal triangles, and the small one is one of them. Its area is a quarter, and its side is half of the big side.
Now, this is important. A length factor isn't an area factor. Sides times root two give areas times two, and sides times two give areas times four.
Learn these three objects by heart. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
